newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court ruling could "paralyse" law making.
newsitem.headline: Italian court ruling could "paralyse" law making.

text.p: Italy's government said on Tuesday a constitutional court ruling which will strip it of a traditional legislative device could paralyse law-making and wipe key measures off the statute books.
The court declared unconstitutional the practice by which cabinets have renewed decree laws, an instrument originally meant only to be applied in extraordinary circumstances.

Deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni said that while the ruling was justified, Italy could face paralysis unless parliament made a mammoth effort to enact more than 50 outstanding "repeat decrees" into law.
"Even correct decisions can have dramatic effects," Veltroni told reporters. "The risk is that we will go into a stall and that risk is very real," he said.
Decrees take immediate effect but lapse unless they are ratified by parliament and passed into law within 60 days.
Successive cabinets, faced with the slow pace of law-making in parliament and filibustering, have in the past simply re-issued decrees with little or no change, renewing their life.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, appointed in May, says it inherited some 100 such repeat decrees and has now slimmed the backlog down to about 50.

Among them are a number on key measures, including provisions that form part of the 1996 budget and arrangements for early retirement for Alitalia staff which are linked to a major restructuring plan at the ailing state airline.
The court's ruling was confirmed by presiding judge Mauro Ferri after a story in the newspaper Corriere della Sera.
Ferri said the ruling would be published within a month.
"The general political effects of the decision are that, from the moment it is published, re-iterating decree laws will become an illegitimate act," Ferri said.

"Once the decision takes effect, I'm not sure whether a government which tries to get round the dispositions of the court will be able to count on the signature of the head of state," he told a news conference.
The Italian president has to sign all legislation, including decree laws. President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro warned in May that he could refuse to sign any re-issued decrees.

Veltroni's alarm at the impact of the court ruling reflects fear that the centre-right opposition could intentionally block passage of repeat decrees to put the government in difficulty and concern at the sheer number that still have to be ratified.
Italian radio said one possible way out was to lump all the decrees in an "omnibus bill", though such a move would require cross-party support or use of risky confidence votes to succeed.
News of the court's ruling broke amid fresh political squabbling over whether to create a new bicameral parliamentary commission to propose reforms to the way Italy is governed.
Part of its job would be to suggest ways to streamline the cumbersome workings of Italy's two houses of parliament.

The Chamber of Deputies and the Senate must approve precisely the same text of any law for it to take effect. Any item of legislation, including decrees, must be examined in various commissions before going before the full assemblies.
